# Mining and Stockpiles {#sec-mining}

::: {.chapter-goal}
#### In this chapter
You will answer the three questions a mine operator, a regulator or an insurer actually asks: how fast is the footprint growing, how much material has moved, and where is the ground hot.
:::

## Three questions, three sensors

Mining work is where remote sensing gets asked for numbers with money attached: a volume for a royalty audit, a footprint for a permit, a hot spot before a stockpile catches fire. Each question needs a different sensor.

| Question | Data | Why that data |
|---|---|---|
| How big is the disturbed area, and how fast is it growing? | Dynamic World, every Sentinel-2 scene | a probability of "bare" every few days, averaged per year |
| How much material has moved? | two elevation models of different dates | the difference, cell by cell, times cell area, is a volume |
| Where is the ground hot? | Landsat 8 and 9 thermal band | 100 m surface temperature, resampled to 30 m, since 2013 |

In commercial work the second question is answered with drone photogrammetry or LiDAR: a DSM at a few centimetres, flown this month, differenced against last month. The logic is identical to what follows; only the resolution and the dates change. Public elevation models give a coarse but real version of the same answer.

::: {.callout-important}
## Scientific integrity: a surface model is not a pit floor
NASADEM (2000) and Copernicus GLO-30 (2011 to 2015) both record the top of whatever was there, including forest canopy. Clearing 25 m tall forest reads as a 25 m "cut". That is why the listing counts only change beyond ±30 m, and only inside today's bare footprint. State the cut-off next to any volume you report, and give the dates of both elevation models, not today's date.
:::

## Heat is a symptom, not a diagnosis

Bare ground is hotter than forest in the dry season whether or not anything is burning, so a raw temperature map is mostly a map of bare ground. The useful signal is persistence: a stockpile that stays hotter than its neighbours pass after pass. Chapter [-@sec-timeseries]'s time series tools turn the map above into that test. A drone thermal flight or a probe on site confirms it.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Change the ±30 m cut-off to ±15 m. How much does the cut volume grow, and how much of that growth is likely cleared forest?
2. Find the hottest 1 % of pixels in the anomaly map. Are they on pits, dumps or stockpile yards?
3. Split the footprint chart into new bare ground and bare ground that has regrown. Which matters more to a regulator?
